short: An allied offensive that stalled against entrenched German positions, marking the beginning of static trench warfare.
full:
Following the German retreat from the Marne, Allied forces launched an offensive on 13 September 1914, intending to drive the enemy out of France. They encountered the German armies reforming on the high ground north of the Aisne River. For the first time, the Germans had dug deep defensive trenches and established overlapping fields of machine-gun fire, rendering traditional infantry assaults ineffective.

The repeated Allied frontal attacks suffered heavy casualties before grinding to a halt by late September. Recognizing that direct assault was impossible, both sides began attempting to outflank each other to the north in a series of maneuvers known as the Race to the Sea. The entrenchments dug at the Aisne became the blueprint for the heavily fortified trench systems that would soon stretch from the Swiss border to the English Channel.
